title: Never Let Me Go — Factual Accuracy Audit
author: Kazuo Ishiguro

issues.location: Ruth's confession section in both L4 and L5 (content_html and flashcard_questions)
issues.claim: Ruth makes a 'deathbed confession' to Kathy and Tommy. Eduqas L4: 'Ruth, now a donor whose body is failing, makes a deathbed confession to Kathy and Tommy.' Eduqas L5 FC5: 'What does Ruth's deathbed confession show?' OCR L4 FC4: 'What confession does Ruth make on her deathbed?' OCR L5 FC5: 'What does Ruth's deathbed confession show?' The term 'deathbed confession' is used consistently across both boards.
issues.correct: Ruth's confession is NOT a deathbed scene. It occurs in Chapter 19 during a car trip to see a beached boat, while Ruth is still alive and communicative (after her first donation, before her second). Ruth gives them Madame's address and confesses she deliberately kept Kathy and Tommy apart. Ruth subsequently completes after her second donation — at that point Kathy sits with her but Ruth 'can't talk' and is not really present; there is no second confession. The confession and the address-giving both happen in the car trip scene, not at a deathbed.
issues.source: Chapter 19 (Kathy drives Ruth and Tommy to see the beached boat, car trip confession); Chapter 20 (Ruth's completion after second donation, no speech). Confirmed via SparkNotes, LitCharts, Shmoop, GradeSaver chapter summaries.

issues.location: Tommy's scream section — presented as direct quotation in content_html and Key Fact boxes
issues.claim: 'His arms were stretched out on either side of him, his head was tilted back, and he was screaming.' Both boards present this as a verbatim quotation from the novel, and both draw the crucifixion analogy directly from this posture.
issues.correct: This phrase does not appear in the novel. The actual Chapter 22 description of Tommy's rage has him 'raging, shouting, flinging his fists and kicking out' in a muddy field, with Kathy catching 'a glimpse of his face in the moonlight, caked in mud and distorted with fury, then I reached for his flailing arms and held on tight.' The novel describes chaotic, uncontrolled flailing — not the composed, symmetrical cruciform posture invented in the lessons. The crucifixion reading is a valid critical interpretation but it should not be attributed to a direct quotation that does not exist. This is a fabricated quote presented as textual evidence.
issues.source: Chapter 22 text confirmed via multiple secondary sources citing the actual passage ('flailing arms', 'face caked in mud'). Zero results for 'arms were stretched out on either side' across all novel databases and academic sources searched.

issues.location: Ruth's confession section — address-giving attributed to deathbed
issues.claim: Eduqas L4: 'She gives them Madame's address and urges them to apply for a deferral.' Presented as part of the 'deathbed confession' scene. OCR L4 FC5: 'What hope does Ruth give Kathy and Tommy for a deferral? That Madame will grant time to couples who can prove they truly love each other.'
issues.correct: The address-giving happens in Chapter 19 (car trip), the same scene as the confession. Ruth hands Madame's address on a piece of paper to Tommy for safekeeping during the car trip. This compounds NLMG-001: not only is the 'deathbed' framing wrong, but the specific detail of giving the address is placed in a scene that does not exist.
issues.source: Chapter 19 summary from SparkNotes, Shmoop, GradeSaver, LitCharts. Ruth gives Madame's address during the car trip on the way to the beached boat.

issues.location: Eduqas L4 content_html Ruth confession section; Eduqas L5 FC4 'Why is Ruth both villain and victim?'
issues.claim: Eduqas L4 quotes Ruth's confession: 'I should have stepped back … I was the one who always wanted Tommy.' This is presented as a direct quotation in the lesson.
issues.correct: This phrasing does not match any verified source for the novel text. Ruth's actual words in Chapter 19 are reported by Kathy as Ruth admitting she kept Kathy and Tommy apart, that 'it should have been you two.' The exact phrasing 'I should have stepped back … I was the one who always wanted Tommy' appears to be a paraphrase or invented quote. No secondary source reproduces this phrasing. The OCR version (FC8: 'I should have been better to you both') is similarly unverified and may derive from the 2010 film rather than the novel.
issues.source: Chapter 19; GradeSaver, SparkNotes, Shmoop quote summaries do not reproduce either version of this phrase as a direct quotation.

issues.location: Judy Bridgewater tape section — Madame's explanation of the dance scene
issues.claim: Eduqas L7: Madame explains she saw 'a new world coming rapidly … and there was this old world, one that we knew was leaving us' — Kathy was clinging to something that would be taken from her. The ellipsis condenses Madame's explanation into this two-clause paraphrase.
issues.correct: Madame's actual speech (Chapter 22) is much more vivid: 'When I watched you dancing that day, I saw something else. I saw a new world coming rapidly. More scientific, efficient, yes. More cures for the old sicknesses. But a harsh, cruel world. And I saw a little girl, her eyes tightly closed, holding to her breast the old kind world, one that she knew in her heart could not remain, and she was holding it and pleading, never to let her go.' The lesson's paraphrase omits 'a little girl, her eyes tightly closed, holding to her breast' — the central image — and also omits 'a harsh, cruel world' which specifies the nature of the 'new world.' The condensed version is misleading as a quotation and loses the most examinable imagery.
issues.source: Chapter 22; Madame's speech confirmed via Goodreads highlights ('When I watched you dancing that day'), SparkNotes, and multiple secondary analyses.

issues.location: Tommy's scream scene — location described as 'after leaving Madame's house' or 'at the roadside'
issues.claim: Multiple lessons describe Tommy's scream as occurring immediately after 'leaving Madame's house' (Eduqas L4 heading: 'After learning the deferral is a myth, Tommy asks Kathy to pull the car over'). The OCR L4 describes the scream as 'into the darkness.' Both lessons describe this as Tommy getting out at 'the roadside.'
issues.correct: Tommy's scream occurs on the drive back from Madame and Miss Emily's house, not at the house itself. He asks Kathy to stop the car, gets out, and rages in a muddy field — at night, with moonlight. He falls in the mud. The scene is in an open field, not a road verge, and there is significant physical detail (mud-caked face, flailing arms, darkness) that the lessons omit. The 'roadside' shorthand is not wrong, but the lessons omit the field setting (the novel says 'muddy field') and Kathy has to wade in after him.
issues.source: Chapter 22 summary from SparkNotes, LitCharts, Shmoop: 'Kathy finds him raging wildly in a muddy field'; 'caught a glimpse of his face in the moonlight, caked in mud.'

issues.claim: Eduqas L3: 'A veteran claims to have spotted a woman in an office in Norfolk who looks like Ruth. The group travels there, and the search ends in failure: the woman looks nothing like Ruth.' OCR L3: similar. Both lessons omit the role of the magazine advertisement — Ruth's dream of the open-plan office is explicitly driven by an office she had seen in a magazine, and the trip arises partly because Rodney has spotted someone who matches this specific image.
issues.correct: The motivation for the trip is more specific: Ruth develops a fantasy of working in an open-plan office after seeing a magazine advertisement. Rodney then spots a woman who resembles Ruth in an open-plan office in Norfolk — a match that seems to fulfil Ruth's fantasy. When they find the woman, she looks nothing like Ruth. The magazine-to-reality link is an important part of Ishiguro's treatment of Ruth's performed identity (she has literally been constructing a dream around a magazine ad). The lessons reduce this to a simple 'spotted woman in office' without the magazine-fantasy context. This is an omission rather than a factual error, but it distorts the significance of the scene.
issues.source: Chapter 13-14 summary; SparkNotes, Shmoop, LitCharts: 'Ruth began to talk about her dream future of working in an open-plan office. The veterans listened eagerly, but Kathy realized that Ruth was describing the office from the magazine.'

issues.location: Norfolk tape section — OCR L3 FC11 and Eduqas L3 content_html
issues.claim: OCR L3 FC11 describes Tommy finding Kathy's tape 'in a Norfolk junk shop.' Eduqas L3 content_html describes Tommy finding the replacement 'in a charity shop.' OCR L3 content_html also says 'Tommy finds a cassette tape of Never Let Me Go by Judy Bridgewater in a Norfolk junk shop.'
issues.correct: The novel's text refers to a 'second-hand shop' or charity shop — multiple secondary sources confirm this. The term 'junk shop' used in OCR L3 content_html is a loose synonym but slightly off-register; 'charity shop' (used in Eduqas and OCR flashcard) is the more accurate description. The discrepancy is minor but the OCR content_html and the OCR flashcard contradict each other on this detail.
issues.source: Chapter 15; LitCharts, SparkNotes, Shmoop all use 'second-hand shop' or 'charity shop.'

issues.claim: Eduqas L1: 'After the third or fourth donation, they complete — a euphemism for death.' (The word complete appears in quotes in the lesson HTML.)
issues.correct: The novel says clones can make up to four donations before completing. Ruth completes after her second donation, suggesting donors do not always reach four. Tommy's fourth donation is treated as unusually significant (characters fear the fourth specifically). The phrase 'third or fourth' implies completing at three is common, but the novel presents the fourth as the threshold that cannot be survived. A more accurate framing is 'up to four donations' — as OCR L4 KC1 correctly states ('up to four'). The Eduqas version implies a range that understates the fourth-donation specificity.
issues.source: Goodreads Q&A and Shmoop chapter summaries confirm: 'No donor makes it past their fourth donation'; Ruth completes after her second. The fourth donation is specifically the one feared.

clean_lessons.notes: Substantially accurate. Dolly the Sheep 1996 correct. Nobel Prize 2017 correct. Boarding school genre analysis sound. 'Told and not told' correctly attributed. Minor issue logged as NLMG-009. Miss Emily's 'How can you ask a world that has come to regard cancer as curable…' quote is a paraphrase of a longer speech but not materially misleading.

Accurate throughout. Madame's spider comparison correctly attributed ('she just froze and waited for us to pass by. She really, really didn't want to be anywhere near us' — the spider simile is student interpretation, correctly presented). Miss Lucy's outburst in the sports pavilion correctly located. Tokens system accurately described. Gallery purpose correctly explained.

Accurate throughout. Three-part structure (Hailsham/Cottages/donations) correctly identified. Bildungsroman analysis sound. Euphemisms (donations/completions/carers/possibles) correctly defined. Reader-as-clone address technique ('I don't know how it was where you were') correctly identified.
